core: Definition of visual hierarchy as the perceived order of importance and the guiding of the eye
Emphasis and the focal point as the mechanism of hierarchy
Primary, secondary, and tertiary levels of hierarchy
Techniques: size/scale, weight, color and contrast, position/placement, whitespace/isolation, alignment, repetition
Reading/scanning patterns (F-pattern, Z-pattern, Gutenberg diagram) with their evidentiary limits
supporting: Gestalt proximity as a grouping principle
Accessibility constraint: do not rely on color alone (WCAG)
outOfScope: Type-specific hierarchy: heading levels, type scale, pairing (belongs to Typography Hierarchy)
Contrast theory as its own subject (Contrast topic)
Balance and distribution of visual weight (Balance topic)
Overall page structure and grid systems (Composition/Layout topics)

claims.claim: Visual hierarchy is the organization of design elements so the eye is guided to take them in in the order of their intended importance.

Emphasis creates a focal point that draws the eye before the rest of a composition, and elements gain or lose emphasis by changing in size, visual intensity, colour, complexity, uniqueness, placement, and relationship to other elements.

Hierarchy is structured into levels: a primary focal point seen first, then secondary, then tertiary elements, allowing the eye to see the first element of importance, then the second, then the third.

Isolation in whitespace and proximity/grouping are emphasis and grouping tools; proximity is a Gestalt principle, and NN/g cites color/contrast, scale, and grouping (proximity, whitespace, enclosure) as means of establishing hierarchy.

The F-shaped reading pattern was identified by the Nielsen Norman Group through eye-tracking research (first reported 2006) and describes readers of unformatted, text-heavy content scanning along the top, a shorter second horizontal sweep, and down the left side; NN/g states it is a default tendency, not a law, and strong cues (headings, bold, images, lists) override it.

The Z-pattern and the Gutenberg diagram are design heuristics grounded in the Western left-to-right, top-to-bottom reading habit; they are presented as patterns/tendencies rather than experimentally validated laws, and both assume even, undifferentiated content and a Western reading direction.

The Gutenberg diagram is attributed to twentieth-century typographer Edmund Arnold and divides a page into a primary optical area (top-left), strong and weak fallow areas, and a terminal area (bottom-right) along a diagonal of 'reading gravity'.
claims.note: Attribution to Edmund Arnold and the four-area labels are consistently reported across secondary design references but not verified against a primary source by Arnold; presented in the lesson as a heuristic and an attribution, not as an experimentally validated claim.

claims.claim: When every element is given equal emphasis, hierarchy collapses and nothing stands out ('If everything is equal, nothing stands out').
Accessibility guidance from the W3C (WCAG) requires that meaning not be conveyed by color alone, which constrains color-based hierarchy cues.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strongly the F/Z/Gutenberg patterns govern eye movement.
positions: Popular design writing sometimes presents these patterns as fixed laws that determine the eye path.
NN/g and the Interaction Design Foundation present them as tendencies/heuristics that depend on content, formatting, and audience, with only the F-pattern backed by eye-tracking data.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows NN/g and IDF: patterns are default tendencies, the F-pattern has eye-tracking support, and the Z-pattern and Gutenberg diagram are heuristics rooted in Western reading order rather than validated laws.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept', 'a simple way to apply it') with no verifiable substantive claims; it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate definitions with a sourced definition of visual hierarchy and emphasis.
Added the specific techniques (size, weight, color/contrast, position, whitespace, alignment, repetition) drawn from the open textbook and NN/g.
Added scanning patterns with explicit attribution and limits rather than asserting them as rules.
rightsIssues: Nielsen Norman Group and Interaction Design Foundation articles are reference-only; their wording was not reproduced, only facts synthesized and attributed.
The BCcampus open textbook is CC BY 4.0; brief quoted phrases are attributed. No copyrighted images, logos, fonts, or proprietary color values were reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Graphic Design and Print Production Fundamentals
sourceRecords.provider: Graphic Communications Open Textbook Collective / British Columbia Institute of Technology (BCcampus Open Education)
sourceRecords.notes: Chapter 3 (Design Elements, Design Principles, and Compositional Organization), sections 3.3 Compositional Principles and 3.4 Organizational Principles. Supports the definitions of emphasis and hierarchy ('hierarchy is applying an order of importance to a set of elements'; a focal point 'draws the eye to it before the eye engages with the rest'; elements 'gain or lose emphasis by changing in size, visual intensity, colour, complexity, uniqueness, placement on the page, and relationship to other elements'), the emphasis-to-hierarchy link, Gestalt proximity, and the 'if everything is equal, nothing stands out' point (quoting Bradley, 2011). The opentextbc.ca host was Cloudflare-blocked to the fetcher; content was read from the identical full-text PDF mirror at bdigital.uvhm.edu.mx. Title, authorship (Graphic Communications Open Textbook Collective, BCIT), and CC BY 4.0 license confirmed via the BCcampus announcement and collection catalog.

sourceRecords.title: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant (Even on Mobile)
sourceRecords.notes: By Kara Pernice, published November 12, 2017. Supports: the F-pattern was identified by NN/g via eye-tracking in 2006 and confirmed in later desktop and mobile studies; it describes fixations concentrated at the top and left; and it is explicitly framed as a default tendency (not a law) that occurs with unformatted text and is broken by headings, bold text, images, and lists. Also supports the recommendation to use formatting to counter it. Reference-only; wording not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Visual Hierarchy in UX: Definition
sourceRecords.notes: By Kelley Gordon, published January 17, 2021. Supports the definition of visual hierarchy ('the organization of the design elements on the page so that the eye is guided to consume each design element in the order of intended importance') and the techniques of color/contrast, scale (recommending few distinct sizes), and grouping via proximity, whitespace, and enclosure. Reference-only; wording not reproduced beyond the short attributed definition.

sourceRecords.title: Visual Hierarchy: Organizing Content to Follow Natural Eye Movement Patterns
sourceRecords.notes: By Mads Soegaard. Supports framing the Z-pattern (for low-text layouts) and F-pattern (for text-heavy content) as scanning patterns/heuristics rather than laws, and the advice to understand the audience before adopting a pattern. Used for the general 'tendencies, not laws' framing and as a secondary reference for the Gutenberg/Z heuristics; the article itself does not discuss the Gutenberg diagram. Reference-only; wording not reproduced.
